newsitem.title: USA: Perdigao's Q1 sets pace for the year.
newsitem.headline: Perdigao's Q1 sets pace for the year.

text.p: Perdigao SA Comercio e Industria's sharp first quarter profit gains have set the pace for all of 1997, according to Chief Executive Nildemar Secches.
"The year is going according to the first quarter," he told analysts on Thursday in New York, the last in a series of meetings with analysts around the U.S. over the past three weeks.
The Brazilian meat producer's first quarter profits were US$10.2 million, up 200 percent from US$3.4 million a year earlier, Chief Financial Officer Wang Wei Chang said.
Gross sales rose 27.6 percent to $277.2 million, he said.
Net sales -- excluding returns -- rose 29.2 percent to $247.1 million. Income before financial results was up 33.3 percent to $10.4 million, Chang said.

Both officials declined to provide second quarter specifics, but Secches pointed out that, on an annual basis, the second quarter is "by far the worst," while the fourth quarter is "by far the best." The first and third quarters are about the same, between the extremes, he said.
On cost projections for the year, Chang said Perdigao expect corn costs to be down about 10 percent from 1996 levels.
He said soybean costs are expected to rise less than five percent.

Noting the company will report first half results using U.S. generally accepted accounting practices (GAAP) in August, Seeches said this "will present a better value than Brazilian GAAP (because) depreciation is lower."

He also said this is the last step needed before registering the company's ADRs for trading in the U.S., although the company has no present plans to file with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.

Still to be worked out, Chang said in response to analysts' questions, is how to increase the liquidity of the company's common stock, 78.3 percent of which is held by eight pension funds. He said the pension fund holdings represent 60.4 percent of the company's total capital, including its preferred shares.

Next week, Chang said, Perdigao will announce the final step in the restructuring begun when present management took over in 1994. This last step involves a series of mergers that will allow the company to use tax loss carryforwards held by subsidiaries.
If these transactions are not completed by the end of June, he said, the company will have to pay $25-$26 million of additional income taxes in future.
Perdigao is still selling non-operating assets, including small pieces of real estate, Secches said.
The company believes it has arranged the sale of the Sao Paulo mansion that once served as company headquarters, he said.
